a47.speaker: Gloria Togbah, fish smoker, Small Fanti Town, Grand Bassa County
a47.speech: "What to do? We just have to sit by the fish because you do not want the fish to spoil when you leave."

a47.speaker: Dr. Philip Z. Ireland, public health specialist, John F. Kennedy Medical Health Center
a47.speech: Said prolonged exposure to smoke affects the lungs and leads to death: "If you are exposed to a huge volume of smoke, it affects the respiratory system." Recommended smoking fish in open, well-ventilated areas to reduce exposure to harmful smoke. "Because of the long exposure to smoke, these women will come down with breathing difficulties and asthma attacks."

a47.speaker: Nathaniel Blama, former Executive Director, Liberia Environmental Protection Agency
a47.speech: Expressed concern over the declining state of Liberia's mangroves and forests cut down for fish smoking; worried that if nothing is done to halt illegal harvesting, the country might lose habitat home to some of the world's endangered species.

a47.speaker: US Environmental Protection Agency (cited)
a47.speech: Cited as the source for finding that traditional fish-smoking methods expose women to respiratory illnesses such as bronchitis, asthma, eye itching, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).

a47.speaker: World Health Organization, 2023 Health and Environmental Scorecard for Liberia (cited)
a47.speech: Found that 52 percent of deaths from stroke and heart disease in Liberia were caused by air pollution.

a47.speaker: Environmental Justice Foundation (EJF), "Leaving No One Behind" report, 2023 (cited)
a47.speech: Found that although the fishery sector is dominated by women, there is little visibility of women in fisheries leadership, particularly over decisions on fish pricing; men are centered on ownership and control of fishing inputs. Recommended addressing gender inequalities in the fisheries sector to enable women to participate fully and improve growth.

a47.speaker: Musu Dorley London, EJF Technical Officer for Gender and Community Participation
a47.speech: Said for so long, women were not included in fisheries governance, and that the Village Savings Loan Association (VSLA) is a platform that empowers women in fisheries governance. "There are a lot of women that own canoes now due to the VSLA." "Women initially did not have money, so when they started to save, they started to gain relevance, and it even helped to bring them together."

a47.speaker: Monica Wood, fish seller, Small Fanti Town, Grand Bassa County
a47.speech: Said the smoke has affected her eyes, and she struggles to breathe sometimes.

a47.speaker: Evelyne Wah, fish seller, Popo Beach, New Kru Town
a47.speech: Said waking up as early as 2 a.m. to buy fish from fishermen has been the greatest barrier: "It's tough and risky for us. Waking up early, sitting in the cold."

a47.speaker: Dorcas Weah, Chairlady, Fanti Town, Marshall, Margibi County
a47.speech: Described the FAO fish-processing facility as a boost that helps them leave the traditional smoking method: "The old way is not good for us. This one is fast, and it can't take a long time." Added that they use the facility only based on customer orders, and complained that operating it is too expensive due to materials like coal, packaging, oil and seasoning.

a47.speaker: Oretha Nimely, Fish for Living Women VSLA, Grand Bassa County
a47.speech: Expressed concern about the maintenance and sustainability of her group's FAO fish-processing facility: "What if something spoils here? We need to fix it. We need money to buy the fish and material to use to dry them."

a47.speaker: Ruth Gbatoe, Communication Officer, Liberia Sustainable Management of Fisheries (LSMF) Project
a47.speech: Said in an email that the project will "comprise training and demonstration in adopting climate-smart practices, including using energy-efficient equipment and solar-powered chill storage in better product handling, especially in fish smoking and drying technology as well as packaging to enhance shelf life with solar-powered cold storage."

a47.speaker: Mike Olendo, Director, Blue Ocean Program, Conservation International
a47.speech: Said "The overall budget for this component is $2 million, with $800,000 allocated to grants (direct cash to women fishmongers) and $800,000 for building their capacity and skills. Overall, it is envisioned that 70% of the funds will be for small grants and 30% for large grants. The project targets approximately 2,000 women fishmongers in four counties: Montserrado, Margibi, Grand Bassa, and Grand Cape Mount."

a229.speaker: Lillian Nalwoga, Chair of the Multistakeholder Advisory Group of the African Internet Governance Forum
a229.speech: Welcomed the holding of this Forum which, for the first time, reached this scale and which was an opportunity for governments, consumers, the private sector, civil society and academics to discuss improving access to the internet for the great benefit of Africa. "We want to take part in the global agenda on internet governance in order to improve digital transformation in Africa. We want to have a secure agenda for Africa," said Ms Nalwoga.

a229.speaker: Dr Macter Seck, Head of the Technology and Innovation Section of the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa (ECA)
a229.speech: Said the internet constitutes an opportunity for the development of the African continent; digital transformation is an imperative for Africa if it wants to reach the SDGs, the African Union's Agenda 2063 and the continental market (AfCFTA); while COVID-19 accelerated digital transformation, Africa is still lagging behind with 40% of its population covered by internet (and an 11% gap between men and women), against a world average of 60%; added that cybersecurity represents about 20 billion dollars of Africa's gross domestic product (GDP), besides being used by terrorists in the Sahel.

a229.speaker: Dr Macter Seck, Head of the Technology and Innovation Section of the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa (ECA)
a229.speech: Insisted that to face this online crime and succeed in the digital transition, the continent must strengthen South-South and North-South partnership, because it needs all actors for the implementation of the African digital strategy ; confided that the ECA will play its part in supporting Africa, through the establishment of centres of excellence for digital technology, a centre of excellence for artificial intelligence (AI), and an initiative to build the capacities of parliamentarians.

a229.speaker: Prof. Umar Garba Danbatta, Vice-President of the Nigerian Communications Commission (NCC)
a229.speech: Noted that the challenges for the continent in internet governance are enormous, and that faced with these challenges, African institutions and States must not remain static; they must follow the momentum, adopt the appropriate laws and regulations, and develop the infrastructure necessary for the deployment of digital technology on the continent ; said his country, Nigeria, is engaged in this approach through the project to set up a digital park in each State, eight of which are already functional.

a229.speaker: Dr Bosun Tijani, Nigerian Minister of Communications, Innovation and the Digital Economy
a229.speech: In his view, the Nigerian government's commitment is in line with the vision of the Internet Governance Forum; with its large population, digital technology constitutes an opportunity for Africa not only as a consumer but also with regard to its capacity to innovate; to get there and boost the future of Africa's digital transformation, a collaborative approach is essential for African States, the minister concluded.

a297.speaker: European Union (statement)
a297.speech: Noted that more than 1.5 million people have been displaced from their homes since 2018 and that between 2024 and 2025 no fewer than 6,900 lives had been lost and over 400,000 people displaced; "This EU funding will support, for a period of six months, and in partnership with the IOM, efforts to implement activities in sectors such as protection, shelter, water, sanitation, and hygiene, as well as multi-purpose financial aid." ; "Escalating armed violence in Benue State, Nigeria, has displaced thousands of people, exacerbating an already critical humanitarian crisis. In June 2025, a wave of attacks forced almost 23,000 people to flee, many of whom had already been displaced in the past, triggering a cycle of heightened vulnerability." ; "Conditions inside the camps are dire. There is a severe lack of shelter for families, and inadequate access to water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH). Access to livelihoods remains precarious, while protection risks have increased considerably, particularly for women, children, and people with disabilities, making the humanitarian response even more complex." ; "This latest wave of violence is part of a protracted humanitarian crisis that has been shaking the state of Benue since 2018... The escalation of violence in 2024 and 2025 has already claimed some 6,900 lives and displaced more than 400,000 people, stressing the urgency of the situation."

a316.speaker: Council of Ministers of Benin (official communiqué signed by Eugène Dossoumou, Secretary General of the Government)
a316.speech: Records that the Council of Ministers met in ordinary session on Wednesday 28 September 2011 and observed a minute of silence in memory of seven deceased persons, including Dah Djihossonou H. Michel Ahanhanzo-Glele, relatives of several members of the National Assembly, and Georges N. Timanty, former Ambassador of Benin to Havana.

a316.speaker: Council of Ministers of Benin (official communiqué)
a316.speech: Announced the adoption of several draft decrees, notably on the creation, powers, composition and functioning of the ad hoc Committee to conduct the process of creating Benin's Court of Auditors; granting approval to “Elavagnon et Fils” Sarl under regime “A” of the investment code for a pipe factory at Bazounkpa; granting approval to the Société des Huileries du Bénin - Bohicon under regime “B” for the extension of its edible oil factory at Bohicon; and on the conditions for the 2011-2012 shea nut marketing campaign.

a316.speaker: Council of Ministers of Benin (official communiqué)
a316.speech: Set the conditions of the 2011-2012 shea nut campaign - a floor producer price of 70 CFA francs per kilogramme, opening on 1 September 2011 and closing on 31 May 2012 - and highlighted the serious depredations of shea that risk penalising future production, namely the absence of a shea sector, the uncontrolled felling of trees and poor preservation of nuts causing excessive acidity ; instructed ministers to ensure strict compliance with the campaign conditions, to continue awareness-raising and training of women marketing and processing shea nuts on better storage, and to undertake a bold reform of the Directorate of Forests and Natural Resources to strengthen protection of shea and néré.

a316.speaker: Council of Ministers of Benin (official communiqué)
a316.speech: Examined and approved several reports, including a joint report by the Ministers of the Interior and of Foreign Affairs on a ministerial delegation's working visit to Iran; a report by the Minister of Economy and Finance on the 2nd review of the economic and financial programme supported by the IMF; a report by the Minister of Nursery and Primary Education on the Ifadem financing agreement signed in Paris; a report by the Minister of Decentralisation on the Decnet 2011 forum in Bujumbura; a report by the Minister of Foreign Affairs on the Bamako workshop on ratification of the African Charter on Democracy, Elections and Governance; and a report by the Minister Delegate for the Maritime Economy on steps to finance consolidation works on investments financed at the Port of Cotonou by the Millennium Challenge Corporation.

a316.speaker: Council of Ministers of Benin (official communiqué)
a316.speech: Examined and approved a communication from the Minister of Higher Education and Scientific Research on creating new faculties at Savè, Tchaourou and Natitingou for the 2011-2012 academic year, responding to the Government's concern to decongest the overcrowded Universities of Abomey-Calavi and Parakou.

a316.speaker: Council of Ministers of Benin (official communiqué)
a316.speech: Authorised, among others, approval of a cooperation agreement with Complant International for bioethanol production from cassava at Savè; the working visit of Ibrahim Assane Mayaki, Director General of the Nepad Planning and Coordinating Agency, for Benin's National Agricultural Investment Programme; Benin's participation in the 13th meeting of States parties to the convention against torture in Geneva, in the 8th Science and Technology in Society forum in Kyoto and in the 62nd UNHCR executive session; the hosting in Cotonou of the 10th Annual General Assembly of the Association of African Road Maintenance Funds; the working visit to Benin of Daniel W. Yohannes, CEO of the Millennium Challenge Corporation, from 9 to 12 October 2011; and the 6th edition of the Civil Society Organisations Days in Cotonou.

a316.speaker: Council of Ministers of Benin (official communiqué)
a316.speech: Pronounced appointments and returns to availability, including a Technical Adviser for Social Affairs at the Presidency of the Republic and directors at the Ministries of Justice, of Higher Education and Scientific Research, and of the Family, Social Affairs, National Solidarity, the Disabled and the Elderly.

a499.speaker: Dr. Mohammad Al-Momani, Jordanian Minister of State for Media Affairs and government spokesperson
a499.speech: Gave a speech at the opening session in which he stressed that "dialogue is not an intellectual luxury, but rather a moral, national and professional necessity and a tool for social peace." He explained that adopting the concept of dialogue in journalistic practice means promoting a culture in which one relies on reliable information, establishing the principle that disagreement does not undermine respect, and that diversity strengthens belonging rather than threatening it. He addressed the participants saying: "You, as media professionals and influencers, bear the responsibility of building a culture of dialogue and resisting hate speech. Take advantage of this opportunity to hone your technical skills and strengthen professional networks based on the belief that words should be a bridge, not a trench."

a499.speaker: Dr. Amer Bani Amer, director of the Hayat Center - Rasid
a499.speech: Stressed that the partnership with KAICIID is in line with the values of joint action to combat hate speech and promote cohesion in the local community. He added that today's meeting, as part of the Journalism Fellowship for Dialogue programme, represents a true investment in the region's future, underlining the urgent need for media capable of serving as a platform for reason and moderation and a space for bridging differences. He explained that the Rasid centre believes that free and responsible expression can heal divisions and promote more inclusive and just societies, noting that the media are not limited to describing reality but rather contribute to reshaping it in a spirit of openness, respect and the values of pluralism and citizenship that embrace diversity.

a499.speaker: Professor Wassim Haddad, director of programmes for the Arab region at KAICIID
a499.speech: Noted that the centre works through dialogue to promote peace and build social cohesion, stressing that the media are a strategic partner in this process. He explained that the Journalism Fellowship for Dialogue programme seeks to broaden knowledge of dialogue in the media, making the media an effective tool for spreading a culture of accepting others and celebrating the region's cultural diversity as a source of enrichment, not conflict.

a1090.speaker: Hillary Rodham Clinton, US Secretary of State, and Leon Panetta, US Secretary of Defense (joint communiqué)
a1090.speech: Announced the establishment of this humanitarian assistance on 27 October, one week after the official end of Muammar Gaddafi's regime ; "After months of fighting and sacrifice, the Libyans have liberated their country with the support of the United States and the international community. The violent dictator and his regime have collapsed. But Libya's newly won freedom was bought at the price of human lives and suffering. Just as the United States and the international community stood alongside the Libyan people during the revolution, they will continue to work with Libya to address humanitarian needs." ; "On Saturday, at the request of the National Transitional Council, the United States will take charge of 24 seriously wounded Libyan fighters transferred to Spaulding Hospital in Boston, Massachusetts. Six other critical cases will be transferred to Germany to be treated there immediately. All these patients were wounded during the fighting that allowed the Libyan people to liberate their country and they suffer from injuries that cannot be treated in Libya." ; "The United States is carrying out their medical evacuation as a humanitarian gesture, a modest symbol of our support, because we are committed to Libya's future. We will remain in solidarity with the Libyan people and we support them, as a partner and a friend, as they build a new and democratic future."

a1090.speaker: Gene Cretz, US Ambassador to Libya
a1090.speech: Made known, as quoted in the Tripoli press on 29 October, that the United States took this measure in response to the request of the National Transitional Council (CNT), Libya's interim government ; "When she came to Tripoli last week, the Secretary of State met some of Libya's war wounded and she saw the extent of the needs with her own eyes."

a1128.speaker: John Mut Bol, Director General in the Unity State Ministry of Health
a1128.speech: Said the number of suspected cases stand at 7,496 with 157 related deaths as of January 1; said in an interview with Eye Radio that the state health ministry had received 225,000 cholera vaccines from the national ministry of health; he however stated that the supply might only cover the epicenter of the outbreak in Bentiu, Rubkona and the Protection of Civilians (POC): "These vaccines will only cover Bentiu town, Rubkona and the PoC. It will not really reach to other places that are far from Bentiu that are affected by the disease." ; Appeals to partners for more supplies to cover the outskirt of the state: "We really urge the partners and also the national ministry of health to push for more vaccines so that other counties like Panyijar, Koch and Mayom can also receive some consignment of these vaccine." ; "It's actually good to also contain the spread of the disease in these other places before the spread of the disease worsens or deteriorate because when it goes to the level that we saw in Rubkona and Bentiu, it will really cost a lot of lives." ; Said the epicenters in Rubkona and Bentiu are starting to report declining number of new infections while the outbreak is increasing in the rural areas.

a1128.speaker: United States Embassy in Juba (press statement)
a1128.speech: On December 31, 2024, said it was joining force with humanitarian partners – through U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) – to help address the ongoing cholera outbreak in South Sudan; said it was providing funding to UN agencies and medical charity MSF to deliver emergency water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) services and provide life-saving medical care; other priority measures include supporting vaccination campaigns, provision of treatment kits and diagnostic tests, and raising public awareness to curb the spread of cholera.

a1128.speaker: Health Pooled Fund
a1128.speech: According to Health Pooled Fund, access to healthcare service remains a challenge for many communities in South Sudan, and even reaching a health facility does not guarantee access to appropriate care.

a1128.speaker: Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF)
a1128.speech: According to MSF, persistent chronic gaps in healthcare, funding cuts, dire water and sanitation conditions and gaps in other essential services in South Sudan have created the perfect conditions for cholera to spread ; MSF stated that the outbreak is getting worse for people living in IDPs camps who have faced appalling conditions for many years, which have continued to deteriorate as donor funding has diminished.

a1422.speaker: Livingstone Masija, Director of the Arusha Society for the Protection of Animals (ASPA)
a1422.speech: According to him, the donkeys cross into Kenya through a number of permeable routes dotting the entire northern borderline, stretching from Loliondo in Arusha, all the way to Tanga ; "Tanzania has banned the slaughter and consumption of donkeys, and the result is that people smuggle them out of the country into Kenya for export to Asian countries but especially China," said Masija, speaking in Arusha during the Workshop on Promoting Animal Welfare Laws and Addressing the Donkey Hide Trade in Tanzania.

a1422.speaker: Livingstone Masija, Director of the Arusha Society for the Protection of Animals (ASPA)
a1422.speech: Warned recently that the main culprit behind donkeys' disappearance was demand for their hides that produce gelatin to make some highly sought-after, traditional Chinese medicine.

a1422.speaker: Livingstone Masija, Director of the Arusha Society for the Protection of Animals (ASPA)
a1422.speech: "Donkey hides business in Tanzania started in 2014 after special abattoirs to slaughter such animals were established in Dodoma and Shinyanga Regions," pointed out Masija ; said that while people don't eat donkeys in Tanzania, their meat is sometimes mixed with ordinary beef to boost volume after the animals are slaughtered for their hides.

a1422.speaker: The Donkey Sanctuary (2020 report)
a1422.speech: In its 2020 report, claimed that nearly 5 million donkey hides were needed to satisfy the high demand for gelatin.

a1422.speaker: Abdinego Martin, communications officer of the Arusha Society for the Protection of Animals (ASPA)
a1422.speech: Pointed out that the importance of donkeys in driving the rural economies cannot be downplayed and the country may suffer drastic consequences if these important animals were left to go extinct; appealed to the media to help raise awareness of the predicament facing the donkey populations in the country.

a1422.speaker: Other experts at the workshop (anonymous)
a1422.speech: It was explained by other experts here that from 2010, donkey prices around the world started to escalate rapidly and it was soon discovered that the catalyst was the high demand for Chinese traditional elixir (Ejiao).

a1457.speaker: Richard H. Riley, US Ambassador to Somalia
a1457.speech: Revealed during a press conference in Mogadishu that the US government has announced a $28 million contribution to fund the first year of two five-year projects to boost resilience and food security in Somalia ; stated that the programs will help more than 80,000 Somali households in Somalia.

a1637.speaker: Centre for Policy Scrutiny (CPS), policy think tank
a1637.speech: Has called on the government to ensure fiscal discipline, institutional coherence and transparent costing in the implementation of the 24-Hour Economy and the Accelerated Export Development Programme. The centre said policy accountability must guide every stage of the programme's rollout to guarantee transparency, efficiency and value for money ; The CPS, however, cautioned that the programme's success would depend on fiscal prudence, coordination among implementing agencies and transparent reporting to ensure that it contributes meaningfully to national development without worsening the country's debt situation.

a1637.speaker: Adu Owusu Sarkodie, Senior Research Fellow at the Centre for Policy Scrutiny
a1637.speech: Said policy accountability should begin with fiscal transparency and the responsible management of public funds. He explained that while the 24-Hour Economy and Accelerated Export Development Programme were ambitious and potentially transformative, their sustainability depended on disciplined financial planning and open reporting. He said the review sought to provide an independent assessment of the programme's design, fiscal implications and implementation prospects within the country's current economic context.

a1637.speaker: Adu Owusu Sarkodie, Senior Research Fellow at the Centre for Policy Scrutiny
a1637.speech: Expressed concern that the estimated $4 billion cost of the initiative might be understated, as it excluded indirect fiscal risks such as tax waivers, contingent liabilities and administrative expenses. He cautioned that without fiscal discipline and accurate cost disclosure, the programme could exert additional pressure on the country's budget and debt stock. "The government must adopt transparent costing and open fiscal reporting to build credibility and prevent the policy from becoming another burden on public finances," he said.

a1637.speaker: Adu Owusu Sarkodie, Senior Research Fellow at the Centre for Policy Scrutiny
a1637.speech: Urged the Ministry of Finance and implementing agencies to publish detailed cost breakdowns, funding sources and expenditure reports for public scrutiny. "Accountability is not achieved by rhetoric but by opening up the numbers for Ghanaians to see how funds are used and what results are being achieved," he emphasised.

a1658.speaker: Government of Djibouti
a1658.speech: declared a state of emergency on 22 November 2019 and activated its emergency plan.

a1658.speaker: Djiboutian authorities
a1658.speech: requested European assistance via the EU Civil Protection Mechanism, given the urgency.

a1658.speaker: Aidan O'HARA, Ambassador of the European Union to Djibouti and to IGAD
a1658.speech: "The EU stands in solidarity with the people of Djibouti affected by these sudden floods. I thank Austria and France for their assistance through the EU Civil Protection Mechanism. The EU's emergency humanitarian assistance funding will enable the victims to receive everyday consumer goods. We are maintaining our contacts with the Djiboutian authorities and are ready to provide further assistance, if necessary."

a1822.speaker: Peter Adrian Chifukwa, Catholic Bishop of Dedza Diocese
a1822.speech: Delivered a stirring sermon urging Malawians to return to the country's moral and divine roots. "We thank God for the gift of resilience of this nation." ; "The resilience of the people, men and women, old and youth—the gift of not ceasing to hope for a better future. This is what binds us today." ; "The founders of this nation knocked for a new, independent nation. But the independence they craved was not an end in itself. It was a journey for freedom, equality, peace, compassion, justice, and prosperity." ; He called on both the government and citizenry to embrace "true patriotism," and said the time has come for citizens to re-anchor Malawi's development agenda in the values of the Kingdom of God – justice, peace, responsibility and compassion ; "There is no reasonable future for us if we don't prepare for it." ; "Our future is a reflection of all well-meaning efforts, small and great, from each one of us." ; He suggested that Malawi's progress hinges not only on economic policies or foreign aid but on a collective spiritual and moral reawakening—a "recollection and renewal" of national purpose, and challenged Malawians to ask themselves what kind of future they hope for, cautioning that a better future is not possible without deliberate positive action.

a1822.speaker: Biziwick Nkhoma, Reverend, Moderator of CCAP General Assembly
a1822.speech: Delivered a sermon steeped in biblical references and nationalistic tone, as much a call to faith as a plea for God's mercy, prompting leaders and citizens alike to rethink their roles in shaping the nation's future. "We knock for a spirit of recollection and renewal so that we may seek for a nation that grows stronger… in unity, enjoyment of freedoms responsibly, and in the spirit of fear of God, justice and peace, opportunities for all, and prosperity."

a1822.speaker: Lazarus Chakwera, President of Malawi
a1822.speech: Presided over the event and read scriptures from Zechariah 8: 18 to 23.

a1822.speaker: George Chaponda, Leader of Opposition
a1822.speech: Said he was there in spirit (having been absent from the prayers).

a1822.speaker: Firas Raad, World Bank Country Manager to Malawi
a1822.speech: Told Malawi News that one big challenge to Malawi's economic independence has been the lack of transformation from subsistence farming to advanced agriculture, then from advanced agriculture to manufacturing and then to a knowledge economy. "There are also questions around saving and investment, the rates of savings and investment are very low compared to regional peers, especially those countries that have done very well." He said Malawi has an ability to move from where it is currently into a middle-income country, but that will depend on long-term reforms. "It is only over a long period of time can you effect a real change."

a1822.speaker: Bertha Bangara Chikadza, President of the Economics Association of Malawi
a1822.speech: Said while international aid and donor support have played a significant role in addressing immediate needs, several structural issues continue to hinder long-term progress towards economic independence. She too hinted at moral values as critical to Malawi's economic growth. "Governance and institutional challenges such as corruption, weak institutions and inadequate policy implementation are also a major hindrance to development. Aid can be largely ineffective if it is not aligned with sound policies, proper governance, and accountability."

a1881.speaker: Bereket Alemayehu, adjunct lecturer at Addis Abeba University and Market Access and Trade Policy Officer at the UK Department for International Trade in Ethiopia (op-ed author)
a1881.speech: writes that to effectively benefit society and themselves, businesses in Ethiopia need to adopt a comprehensive approach to CSR, embracing its economic, legal, ethical and philanthropic aspects; he argues that Ethiopian businesses' view of CSR mainly focuses on its philanthropic dimension, a narrow interpretation of the concept, and that firms need to prepare tailor-made CSR objectives and strategies in advance as part of their overall plans.

a1881.speaker: Milton Friedman (stockholder theory)
a1881.speech: The stockholder theory, mainly advocated by Milton Friedman, states that the only social responsibility of businesses is to make a profit, nothing more or less; managers of firms should be concerned with and toil for only maximising shareholder value.

a1881.speaker: Edward Freeman (stakeholder theory)
a1881.speech: The stakeholder theory, propounded by such scholars as Edward Freeman, asserts that as businesses' operations impact many stakeholders other than its stockholders, they have responsibilities towards all stakeholders, including their owners.

a1881.speaker: Archie Carroll, “Carroll’s CSR Pyramid” (cited framework)
a1881.speech: According to the widely cited “Carroll’s CSR Pyramid”, the responsibilities are broadly categorised as economic, legal, ethical and philanthropic, put in a bottom-up order in a pyramid diagram.

a1881.speaker: Paul Hohnen’s work and other studies (cited research)
a1881.speech: Many studies, such as Paul Hohnen's work, reveal the positive relationship between a company's discharge of CSR and its enhanced profitability, such as through building its reputation in the market — commonly referred to as the “business case for CSR”.

a1881.speaker: UN Global Compact / UN Sustainable Development Goals (instruments cited)
a1881.speech: The UN Global Compact promotes CSR through its 10 principles that guide the operation of companies, focusing on human rights, labour, the environment and anti-corruption; the UN Sustainable Development Goals also recognise the crucial role of businesses in meeting the Goals.

a1881.speaker: Ethiopia’s new Investment Proclamation (legal document)
a1881.speech: The Proclamation obliges investors to comply with laws and give due regard to social and environmental sustainability values, including environmental protection and social inclusion.

a1936.speaker: Moustapha Mohamed Mahamoud, Minister of National Education and Vocational Training of Djibouti
a1936.speech: "Every child, whether able-bodied or living with a disability, has the right to flourish in a school environment that values their abilities and protects their dignity," he stated in a declaration made during the launch of the workshop on school harassment. He also called for a cultural paradigm shift, insisting on the importance of seeing disability not as a limitation but as a form of ability deserving respect and support.

a1936.speaker: Doualeh Said Mahamoud, Director General of the National Agency for Persons with Disabilities (ANPH)
a1936.speech: "We have a role to play, not only as educators, but also as citizens, to eradicate stigma and promote tolerance."

a1936.speaker: Doualeh Said Mahamoud, Director General of the National Agency for Persons with Disabilities (ANPH)
a1936.speech: On the new orthopaedic fitting and rehabilitation centre at the Cheiko hospital in Balbala: "this represents hope, a promise of mobility and dignity for hundreds of Djiboutian families who, until now, faced insurmountable obstacles in accessing specialised care."

a1952.speaker: Hamadou Issaka, Director of the Institute of Research in Human Sciences (IRSH)
a1952.speech: In his welcome message, underlined the importance of the role of religious leaders in the socio-spatial reconfiguration of the Alliance of Sahel States (AES) and recalled that this meeting follows on from the reflections conducted at the conference of 16 January on sovereignty in the AES area; he insisted on the strong religiosity that characterises the AES area, where the message of religious leaders carries an almost absolute authority: “We are a community of believers and of beliefs in which the message of the religious leader is often confused with the words of the Gospel.”

a1952.speaker: Hamadou Issaka, Director of the Institute of Research in Human Sciences (IRSH)
a1952.speech: Warned of attempts at destabilisation by certain occult forces seeking to undermine this ancestral harmony: “For some years now, individuals with malicious intentions have appeared and are trying to call into question the good neighbourliness that has always characterised our communities.” ; “Who better than religious leaders, those who preach the true divine word, to bring those who have strayed back onto the right path,” he asked, recalling that this guidance is a religious obligation and citing the Quran (3:110): “You are the best community that has been raised up for mankind. You enjoin what is right and you forbid what is wrong.”

a1952.speaker: Hamadou Issaka, Director of the IRSH (citing the IRSH 2019 study)
a1952.speech: Recalled that the results of the IRSH’s 2019 study on interreligious and intercultural coexistence in six regions of Niger attest to a tradition of tolerance: “Cohabitation takes place peacefully, with respect for each person’s values.” ; “Muslims and Christians regularly visit one another for their respective major religious festivals,” he added.

a1952.speaker: IRSH study (2019) on interreligious and intercultural coexistence in six regions of Niger
a1952.speech: Its results attest to a tradition of tolerance, showing that cohabitation takes place peacefully, with respect for each person’s values.

a1952.speaker: Observatory of Religious Life (2018 report)
a1952.speech: Noted that relations between Muslims and Christians in Niger are traditionally good.

a1952.speaker: Hamadou Issaka, Director of the IRSH
a1952.speech: In conclusion, expressed his optimism regarding the discussions, which should lead to “proposals and recommendations capable of guiding us further towards the right path, which is distinct from wandering astray.”

a1952.speaker: Mauro Armanino, representative of the University of the Common Good (UBC)
a1952.speech: Recalled that the UBC was born in response to the attacks on Christian places of worship in January 2015, seen as a sign of the shrinking of spaces for social dialogue, and explained that to remedy this situation the UBC set itself the mission of creating spaces for “calm, responsible and constructive” debate “between intellectuals and social operators”.

a1952.speaker: Mauro Armanino, representative of the University of the Common Good (UBC)
a1952.speech: Insisted on the complexity of the relations between religion and politics: “We know from experience that this relationship is not self-evident. On the contrary, it is an ambiguous relationship…”, highlighting the risks of the sacralisation of power; he illustrated his point with recent examples from the United States, citing former president Donald Trump: “Trump claimed that God saved him from the attack in order to restore America’s greatness… Then he began to expel migrants and to put them in chains… Is this too the will of God?” He also questioned the legitimacy of the presidential pardons granted by Trump and Joe Biden: “God alone grants pardon…”

a1952.speaker: Mauro Armanino, representative of the University of the Common Good (UBC)
a1952.speech: Concluded by warning against the temptation of power to make itself divine: “Let us not forget that all power tends to make itself divine or to be divinised… From the pharaohs to the present day, the power of the chief is almost religious!”, calling on the participants to reflect on the role of religious leaders in the political space.

a1989.speaker: Sunday Dare, President Tinubu's Special Adviser on Media and Public Communication
a1989.speech: Disclosed in a statement on Thursday that the prices of foodstuffs and other essential commodities may never revert to their levels before the removal of fuel subsidies, despite ongoing economic reforms intended to stabilise the economy ; noted that although Nigerians have experienced economic hardship following the removal of fuel subsidies, key indicators suggest that the economy is gradually recovering ; emphasised that while prices may not revert to pre-subsidy levels, they are beginning to stabilise across various sectors: "Yes, prices are not back to the pre-subsidy removal regime. They probably may never be. But prices of foodstuffs and other services are dropping across the board. Multiple independent market surveys have confirmed this development."

a1989.speaker: Sunday Dare, President Tinubu's Special Adviser on Media and Public Communication
a1989.speech: Argued that rebasing is a globally recognised economic practice that enhances the accuracy of economic data, enabling better policy decisions: "Rebasing injects precision into policymaking by providing a panoramic view of a country's economic terrain, exposing both its strong and weak sectors. Vital information to guide investors is also provided."

a1989.speaker: Sunday Dare, President Tinubu's Special Adviser on Media and Public Communication
a1989.speech: Maintained that the reforms were necessary for long-term economic stability: "Under President Tinubu's watch, we are seeing the headwinds abating and a new economic tailwind in favour of economic reforms."

a1989.speaker: National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) report
a1989.speech: Showed that Nigeria's inflation rate has declined from 34.8% to 24.48% year-on-year after rebasing; food inflation stands at 26.08%, core inflation at 22.59%, urban inflation at 26.09%, and rural inflation at 22.15%.

a1989.speaker: The Tinubu administration / Presidency
a1989.speech: Has defended its economic policies, insisting that ongoing reforms in the oil sector and the shift towards local refining have started yielding positive results.

a1989.speaker: Bloomberg Africa report
a1989.speech: Acknowledged that "Nigeria's fortunes appear to be looking up after nearly two years of painful economic reforms and investors are taking notice" ; further suggested that Nigeria could regain its status as Africa's largest economy when rebased Gross Domestic Product (GDP) figures are released next month, potentially pushing the GDP close to $500 billion.

a2021.speaker: Televisão de Moçambique (TVM) and Rádio e Televisão Portuguesa (RTP)
a2021.speech: Express interest in revising the cooperation protocols in order to adjust to the new trends of the television broadcasting market.

a2021.speaker: Nicolau dos Santos, Chairman of the Board (PCA) of RTP
a2021.speech: Opened up opportunities for internships and technical and professional training for TVM workers ; gave the TVM chairman guarantees about the possibility of sending TVM technicians for internships and professional training activities at RTP.

a2021.speaker: Victor Nhatitima, Chairman of the Board (PCA) of TVM
a2021.speech: Seeks support in technologies, knowledge and other opportunities for strengthening institutional capacity for the repositioning of TVM in the market.

a2021.speaker: Mozambican Football Federation
a2021.speech: Guarantees that it is working, at all costs, for the best of the national team, two days before the end of the contract of national football coach Chiquinho Conde; the position was taken on Thursday during a meeting held with the Ministry of Youth and Sports, Caifadine Manasse.

a2021.speaker: Francisco Pagula, Governor of Inhambane
a2021.speech: Defends the consolidation of the cultural and creative industry as one of the main vectors for boosting tourism and local economic development; he was speaking on Thursday during the reception of the runner-up of the international "Miss World Culture 2025" contest, held in Nigeria.

a2021.speaker: President of the Republic (of Mozambique)
a2021.speech: Said, in the speech relaunching the project, that the act represents Mozambique's capacity to overcome challenges and recover the confidence of international investors.

a2021.speaker: First Lady (Gueta Chapo)
a2021.speech: Appeals for the unity of Mozambicans to respond to the needs of families affected by the floods ; says that strengthening cooperation is fundamental to save lives and restore dignity to the victims of calamities.

a2021.speaker: Spokesperson of the PRM (Mozambican Republic Police)
a2021.speech: Said the case — the collapse of an illegal mine that killed five artisanal miners and injured five others in Movinha, Gurúè District, Zambézia Province — happened last Monday.

a2021.speaker: Chief Executive of TotalEnergies
a2021.speech: Announces a donation of 200 million meticais in support of the victims of the floods in the southern and central regions of the country.

a2168.speaker: Henry Kachaje, Chief Executive Officer of the Malawi Energy Regulatory Authority
a2168.speech: Told Parliament that he could not provide a definitive timeline for when fuel supply would stabilise.

a2473.speaker: Nana Yaw Sarpong, Deputy General Secretary of the United Party (UP+) (social media post)
a2473.speech: In a social media post, commended the Bank of Ghana Governor and other key economic managers for what he described as a "renewed confidence in the Cedi" and a "steady appreciation against the dollar in recent months" ; "Initially, I asked myself, why celebrate the Cedi at 60? But after some reflection, it actually makes sense. We are getting a few things right as a nation - the steady appreciation of the Cedi, the welcomed 'rain down' of inflation, the return of investor trust, and signs of stability and growth. Ayekoo to Ghana, and especially to the Bank of Ghana." ; "There is still more work ahead, but for now, let's celebrate the progress!"

a2473.speaker: Dr Johnson Pandit Kwesi Asiamah, Governor of the Bank of Ghana
a2473.speech: Reiterated the central bank's commitment to maintaining stability, noting that the strength of a currency reflects the strength of the nation's discipline, productivity, and unity of purpose.

a2490.speaker: Bill Gates, President of the Gates Foundation
a2490.speech: Exhorted African leaders to accelerate progress in health and development through innovation and partnership, despite the obstacles, in a speech delivered on Monday 2 June in the Nelson Mandela Hall at African Union headquarters; announced that the bulk of the $200 billion he is donating from his own fortune will be devoted over the next 20 years to Africa, with an emphasis on collaboration with governments that prioritise the health and well-being of their citizens ; stressed the essential role that African leadership and ingenuity will play in building the continent's health and economic future: "By unlocking human potential through health and education, every country in Africa should be able to take the path to prosperity, and that is an exciting adventure to which I want to contribute."

a2490.speaker: Bill Gates, President of the Gates Foundation
a2490.speech: Called for priority to be given to primary health care, insisting on investment in this area: "helping a mother to be healthy and well nourished before and during pregnancy, and then making sure that the child receives good nutrition during his or her first four years, makes all the difference."

a2490.speaker: Dr Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala, Director-General of the World Trade Organization, and Amina J. Mohammed, UN Deputy Secretary-General
a2490.speech: Issued calls for collaboration and shared responsibility; according to them, Africa's progress in health is the fruit of strong government leadership, resilient communities and partnerships that deliver results.

a2490.speaker: Graça Machel, renowned campaigner for women's and children's rights
a2490.speech: Described the current situation as "a moment of crisis" and stressed the importance of lasting partnerships in Africa's development journey, while emphasising that "Mr Gates's long-standing partnership with Africa reflects a deep understanding of these challenges and a respect for African leadership, its ideas and its innovation."

a2783.speaker: Mayo Clinic (article)
a2783.speech: According to this article from Mayo Clinic, drinking can offer some health benefits, especially for your heart. It can lower your risk of heart disease, stroke and possibly reduce your risk of diabetes - if done in moderation.

a2783.speaker: TIME, citing a study of nearly two million people published in The BMJ
a2783.speech: According to TIME, there is more evidence from a new study of nearly two million people published in The BMJ that moderate amounts of alcohol appear to be healthy for most heart conditions - but not all of them; non-drinkers had an increased risk for eight of the 12 heart ailments studied compared to people who drank in moderation, and a 56% higher risk of dying unexpectedly from heart disease compared to those who enjoyed a glass or two a day.

a2988.speaker: Source at the Maputo High Court of Appeal (anonymous)
a2988.speech: Told Lusa on Wednesday that the son of former Mozambican president Armando Guebuza, sentenced to 12 years in prison in the hidden debt scandal, has been released: "He left the prison where he was being held on Tuesday and is now on parole."

a2988.speaker: Maputo City Court
a2988.speech: Found it proven that the son of former President Guebuza received bribes to influence his father to approve the coastal protection project, which was used to raise money to feed hidden debts. The court also found it proven that six of the 19 official suspects were bribed to facilitate meetings with the former Mozambican president and influence the approval of the coastal protection project used to raise the money that fuelled the hidden debts involving the Privinvest shipyards, and ruled that assets it considered to be "proceeds of crime" from the convicted defendants should be forfeited to the state.

a2988.speaker: Efigénio Baptista, judge in the case
a2988.speech: At the time, explained that Ndambi Guebuza was convicted of the crimes of criminal association and criminal conspiracy, blackmail, influence peddling, forgery, embezzlement and money laundering.

a2988.speaker: Supreme Court source (anonymous)
a2988.speech: "This is conditional release," a Supreme Court source told Lusa on Tuesday.

a2988.speaker: Maputo High Court of Appeal
a2988.speech: In light of the 2019 Penal Code, argued at the time that the convicted woman should serve three quarters of her sentence.

a2988.speaker: Supreme Court of Mozambique (ruling of April 14)
a2988.speech: Ruled that the previous law (2014), which was in force at the time of the crime and the initiation of criminal proceedings, should apply, allowing for parole after serving half of the sentence. ; "It is unreasonable (…) that the official suspect should be surprised by the tightening of criminal law and the enforcement of criminal sanctions at a stage when she has already been charged, indicted, tried and convicted under the previous criminal law."

a2988.speaker: Mozambican public prosecutor
a2988.speech: Discovered in 2016, the debts were estimated at around US$2.7 billion (more than €2.3 billion), according to figures presented by the Mozambican public prosecutor.

a2988.speaker: World Bank
a2988.speech: Mozambique was then one of the ten fastest growing economies in the world for two decades, according to the World Bank.

a3137.speaker: Olusegun Obasanjo, former President of Nigeria and AU mediator
a3137.speech: “Today is the beginning of a new dawn for Ethiopia, for the Horn of Africa and indeed for Africa as a whole. Let me hasten to thank God for this new dawn. We are seeing in practice and actualisation what we have tried to achieve for ourselves over the years - African solutions for African problems” ; “The two parties in the Ethiopian conflict have formally agreed to the cessation of hostilities as well as to systematic, orderly, smooth, and coordinated disarmament, restoration of law and order, restoration of services, unhindered access to humanitarian supplies, protection of civilians especially women, children, and other vulnerable groups, among other areas of agreement. The agreement also takes care of assurance of security for all concerned within and outside Ethiopia.”

a3137.speaker: Ethiopian government and TPLF (joint statement)
a3137.speech: “We have agreed to permanently silence the guns and end the two years of conflict in northern Ethiopia” ; “We have also agreed on a detailed programme of disarmament, demobilisation, and reintegration of the TPLF combatants, taking into account the security situation on the ground” ; both parties conceded that the conflict brought a tragic loss of lives and livelihoods, and both delegations committed to implementing the undertaking without delay.

a3137.speaker: Uhuru Kenyatta, former President of Kenya
a3137.speech: said the high-level panel, which facilitated the talks, stood ready to assist with the implementation of the agreement signed ; “Solutions to the problems of Ethiopia lie in the hands of the people of Ethiopia.”

a3137.speaker: Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka, former South African deputy president
a3137.speech: said that the main thrust of the agreement was aimed at silencing the guns and ending the killings.

a3137.speaker: Naledi Pandor, South African International Relations and Cooperation Minister
a3137.speech: said she was the “most relieved person in the room” following the signing of the agreement ; “When the AU approached us [South Africa], I had to think very hard on the matter. I was initially extremely reluctant, but when I approached President Cyril Ramaphosa, he said, of course, we have to do it, it is our duty to ensure that stability is restored.”

a3137.speaker: Cyril Ramaphosa, President of South Africa (quoted by Naledi Pandor)
a3137.speech: “of course, we have to do it, it is our duty to ensure that stability is restored.”

a3137.speaker: African Union and observer missions, including the United Nations
a3137.speech: hailed the agreement as an effort to end ongoing killings.

a3141.speaker: Dye Mawindo, MCA-M II chief executive officer
a3141.speech: expressed optimism that when completed, the four road corridors will improve access to markets and other strategic zones, thereby paving the way for socio-economic empowerment in the project areas ; “We have locations such as Chantulo, which have arable and productive land, but are underutilised because farmers do not have access to markets. If we can improve the roads, access will improve, transport costs will go down and smallholder farmers will have better economic prospects.”

a3141.speaker: Dye Mawindo, MCA-M II chief executive officer
a3141.speech: said rehabilitating the Golomoti-Monkey Bay Turn-Off section will also boost the tourism sector by connecting Lilongwe and other key tourism sites in Mangochi as well as other lakeshore districts ; however, said there is need for coordination with other key stakeholders such as the Competition and Fair Trading Commission to ensure that transporters offer competitive rates when the projects are completed.

a3141.speaker: Kelvin Mphonda, Ministry of Transport and Public Works director of roads
a3141.speech: said the signing sets the foundation for resource deployment and the initiation of projects critical to enhancing the nation’s transportation infrastructure ; said the project could experience some cost overruns following concerns that the prices quoted in the initial project three years ago might be lower than the required costs, but said this is normal for long-term projects.

a3141.speaker: Matilda Matabwa, Roads Authority board chairperson
a3141.speech: said they intend to use the project’s first phase to determine the real value of the construction works and revise the cost accordingly ; “We are confident that when we approach Millennium Challenge Corporation [MCC] with the revised figures, they will be willing to accommodate us.”

a3252.speaker: Debora Katisa Carvalho, First Lady of Cabo Verde and president of the Dret.u Foundation
a3252.speech: Stated that Sao Vicente today needs the generosity of everyone -- authorities, entities, NGOs, ordinary citizens, tourists, Cape Verdeans in the country and in the diaspora, as well as international partners: "We need a great Djunta Mon movement. What happened in Sao Vicente this past 11 August, with the torrential rains that left a trail of pain and destruction, calls on all of us to bring an embrace of solidarity, a movement of empathy, to all those who lost their loved ones, their belongings and their means of subsistence." ; Emphasized that these people must be helped to rebuild their lives, since many lost their homes and cannot return to them, and said that "as First Lady and president of the Dret.u Foundation, in partnership with the Red Cross of Cape Verde," she was launching the solidarity campaign for Sao Vicente, whose main objective is to support families in a situation of vulnerability, people who lost all their material possessions and in some cases also loved ones.

a3252.speaker: Debora Katisa Carvalho, First Lady of Cabo Verde and president of the Dret.u Foundation
a3252.speech: Underlined that she intends to promote a large civic and community mobilization so that people do not stop visiting the island of Sao Vicente: "There was already an economic, tourist, social and musical movement for the Baia das Gatas Festival, and we would like people to continue mobilizing to go to the island of Sao Vicente, transforming that movement into a musical festival of human values, a great festival of humanity." ; Stated that Cape Verdeans, and Sao Vicente in particular, can be a great example to the world of what a festival of human values should be, marked by empathy, friendship and unity in helping to recover streets still covered with mud and rubble ; Appealed for the involvement of the churches and of the Association of Psychologists of Cape Verde in a national and international Djunta Mon to help the island return to normality.

a3252.speaker: Debora Katisa Carvalho, First Lady of Cabo Verde and president of the Dret.u Foundation
a3252.speech: Said the campaign will be at the national and international level: "We already have many international partners contacting the platform, the Office of the First Lady and the foundation to offer support. We will use all national and international networks, and the Red Cross, to carry out the collection of goods, both material and financial." ; Reported that on 23 August she will take part in Lisbon in a solidarity event called "Um Cuscuz Solidario" at the Cape Verde Cultural Centre: "We want to bring together Cape Verdeans, friends and institutions that have expressed a wish to make donations. In the first week of September, we will be in the United States of America, more specifically in Massachusetts." ; Announced that air and sea operators are already available to transport the donations collected abroad, which will be delivered in Sao Vicente.

a3252.speaker: Debora Katisa Carvalho, First Lady of Cabo Verde and president of the Dret.u Foundation
a3252.speech: Stressed the importance of ensuring that children can return to school normally with the start of the new school year in September: "We appeal to people, nationally and internationally, to donate school supplies, since many families lost everything, including their children's school materials."

a3452.speaker: Save the Children (British non-governmental organisation)
a3452.speech: Warned on Wednesday that without critical action, nearly 230 000 children and new mothers in war-ravaged Sudan are "likely to die from hunger": "Nearly 230 000 children, pregnant women and new mothers could die in the coming months" ; said "more than 2.9 million children in Sudan are acutely malnourished and an additional 729 000 children under five are suffering from severe acute malnutrition -- the most dangerous and deadly form of extreme hunger" ; warned "about 222 000 severely malnourished children and more than 7 000 new mothers are likely to die" under current levels of funding which "only covers 5.5%" of Sudan's total needs.

a3452.speaker: Arif Noor, Save the Children's country director in Sudan
a3452.speech: Said the bombing and destruction of fields and factories have plunged Sudan into "one of the worst" nutrition situations in the world; warned the situation would only worsen as the consequences of the current fighting take hold: "No planting last year means no food today. No planting today means no food tomorrow. The cycle of hunger is getting worse and worse with no end in sight -- only more misery."

a3452.speaker: United Nations
a3452.speech: Says nearly 11 months of fighting between the forces of two rival generals has killed thousands and displaced eight million people in Sudan, and that more than half of all Sudanese, including 14 million children, require humanitarian assistance to survive; has described a "climate of sheer terror", reporting the use of heavy artillery in densely populated urban areas, sexual violence as a weapon of war, and the destruction of hospitals and schools.

a3452.speaker: United Nations World Food Programme (WFP)
a3452.speech: Sounded the alarm on Sudan this month, warning the war risked triggering the world's largest hunger crisis.

a3452.speaker: United States
a3452.speech: Has accused both sides of war crimes and alleged the RSF has carried out ethnic cleansing and crimes against humanity.

a3452.speaker: Report before the UN Human Rights Council
a3452.speech: Details gross violations and abuses of international human rights law and possible war crimes.

a3452.speaker: Volker Turk, UN human rights chief
a3452.speech: Called the conflict a "living nightmare" and said it had "slipped into the fog of global amnesia".

a3452.speaker: Experts
a3452.speech: Have warned the conflict could last years.

a3517.speaker: Hamza Abdi Barre, Prime Minister of the Federal Government of Somalia
a3517.speech: Expressed gratitude to China for its continued support to Somalia, particularly in the areas of politics, security cooperation, economic development, and humanitarian assistance.

a3517.speaker: Wang Yu, Ambassador of the People's Republic of China to Somalia
a3517.speech: Highlighted the longstanding partnership between Somalia and China and reaffirmed his country's commitment to further supporting the Somali people and government.

a3696.speaker: Saturn Corporation Limited
a3696.speech: The company, which currently assembles Chinese-made heavy duty trucks, says the move responds to growing demand across key sectors including agriculture, mining and regional transport.

a3696.speaker: Rehballah Habib, Managing Director of Saturn Corporation
a3696.speech: “We have seen a growing need for pickups, around July or August next year, we will begin assembling pickups with capacities of 1 tonne and 1.5 tonnes” ; said this expansion complements its existing lineup of vehicles already utilised in Tanzania’s mineral-rich and agricultural regions, as well as for cross-border transport to neighbouring countries such as the Democratic Republic of Congo, Burundi, Malawi and Zimbabwe.

a3732.speaker: Dr Annelie Rabie, Overstrand Mayor
a3732.speech: Said they evacuated families in Sea Farm, where four properties were destroyed, and temporarily relocated them to Kleinmond town hall ; “Some went to their families and relatives in other areas. We have three families staying at the community hall. Many of the affected houses are holiday homes and are not usually occupied” ; said the municipality responded to six fires in different areas, including Masakhane, which has been extinguished, and Sea Farm.

a3732.speaker: A resident in Betty's Bay (anonymous)
a3732.speech: Told News24 she was preparing for evacuation amid the blazing fire; said some residents had evacuated their homes to friends, relatives or the Kleinmond town hall at the instruction of authorities from the Overstrand municipality. “There are people who have evacuated. It's started to rain, but the rain is not enough, and the flames are still quite high. We hope the rain will put out the fire. Otherwise, we're all packed and ready to go if they say we must leave. It is just a matter of waiting and seeing where the fire goes. The wind is blowing” — adding that she would wait “until the last moment” to leave her home.

a3732.speaker: SA Weather Service (SAWS)
a3732.speech: Issued several yellow-level two warnings on Monday for damaging winds, damaging coastal winds and thunderstorms for the central and northern parts of the Western Cape and the southern parts of the Northern Cape.

a3732.speaker: Grant Cohen, Speaker of the Overstrand Municipality
a3732.speech: Said the municipality had declared code red, meaning the blaze directly threatened the resident's safety ; “Households in Silversands, Sunny Seas, Seafarms and Blesberg are asked to prepare for evacuation from their homes because of the wildfire.”

a3732.speaker: Cape Winelands municipality
a3732.speech: “The only fire line where progress in securing the line has been made is the Elandsberg line.”

a3732.speaker: Jermaine Cerelse, Cape Town fire services spokesperson
a3732.speech: Said Cape Town firefighters extinguished fires in Vrygrond, Masiphumelele, Broadlands and Overcome Heights earlier in the day.

a3732.speaker: Charlotte Powell, City of Cape Town disaster risk management centre spokesperson
a3732.speech: Said the fires at Overcome Heights Informal settlement destroyed about 40 structures, leaving 150 displaced; said a 12-year-old boy received treatment for burn wounds ; “Infrastructure damage includes standpipes, portable toilets and electrical infrastructure. The relevant City services will be activated to assist in this regard” ; “Our NGO partners will provide humanitarian assistance, and various City departments will assess the damaged infrastructure.”

a3751.speaker: Eric Bougouma, Minister of Infrastructure of Burkina Faso
a3751.speech: Said the roadway will be 7m wide with two 1.5m shoulders on either side in open country and 8m wide with 2m shoulders through built-up areas ; “This infrastructure will mobilise 71 million US dollars, or about 42 billion CFA francs” ; said the road will be built to international standards in bituminous concrete: “It will be of higher quality than the Dédougou-Tougan road built with a double surface dressing.”

a3751.speaker: Eric Bougouma, Minister of Infrastructure of Burkina Faso
a3751.speech: Noted a delay in the execution of the project, saying preparation of the project took 20 months and 30 months are planned for the execution phase ; “A mission of the Saudi Fund was postponed to March because of the closure of borders due to COVID-19” ; made known that discussions are under way to finalise certain files, in particular the choice of the consultant who will carry out the review of the study and draw up the tender documents for the firms to be selected.

a3751.speaker: Salif Ouédraogo, Minister of Agriculture and Hydro-Agricultural Development of Burkina Faso
a3751.speech: Presented three bills to the National Assembly; said the PAFA-4R project, financed as a loan by the International Fund for Agricultural Development (IFAD) to the tune of 52 billion CFA francs, will allow the development of 2,000 ha of lowlands, the creation of 1,600 rural micro-enterprises and will emphasise support to women in their access to land ; “The two financings amount to 32 billion CFA francs which will allow the development of 1,400 ha of land through full water control at the Léraba, the creation of 1,500 rural micro-enterprises, and the construction of 38 storage warehouses and a purchasing counter” ; “They will allow the farmers of these lands to have sufficient means of production and to increase the domestic processing of output. These are structuring projects that will improve food security in our country.”

a3815.speaker: Mike Elvis Tusubira, motorcycle taxi rider living with HIV in Uganda
a3815.speech: says he will have to split up from his wife as they can no longer have safe sex: “It means that even my marriage will end, because actually without the preventive measures, she’s not going to stay” ; “No condoms, no [anti-HIV] lubricants, no PrEP, nothing. We can’t stay in marriage without meeting. It means that I have to stay single.”

a3815.speaker: Mike Elvis Tusubira, motorcycle taxi rider living with HIV in Uganda
a3815.speech: said he phoned his counsellor at the Kiswa Health Centre III to find out what was going on: “My counsellor was in the village. He told me that he is no longer at the clinic” ; “I’m moving in the dark, in the darkness. I don’t know whether my viral load is suppressed. I’m traumatised” ; “Some other people say that the drugs will be in private pharmacies... as a boda-boda rider I don’t know whether I can raise the money to sustain my treatment.”

a3815.speaker: Mike Elvis Tusubira, motorcycle taxi rider living with HIV in Uganda
a3815.speech: says they have also been impacted by the loss of services provided by NGOs that received funding from USAID, his wife getting her PrEP via an NGO at Marpi and his five-year-old son benefitting from one that provided school and food for vulnerable children: “My child is no longer at school now” ; “At least it will be a bit simpler. If I die, they just bury me there, instead of disturbing my people here in Kampala. Because I have no way I can live here without ARV services.”

a3815.speaker: Dr Shamirah Nakitto, clinician with Reach Out Mbuya (Rom), Uganda
a3815.speech: “We are waiting for the 90 days. So, this compulsory leave, I hadn’t prepared for it” ; “It was so abrupt. We didn’t have a proper handover at the facility. We just stopped working.”

a3815.speaker: Uganda’s health ministry
a3815.speech: says it is exploring ways to minimise disruptions.

a3815.speaker: Dr Diana Atwine, top civil servant at Uganda’s health ministry
a3815.speech: urged staff “willing to continue working in the spirit of patriotism as volunteers” to get in contact.

a3815.speaker: US government data
a3815.speech: According to US government data, Uganda received $295m (£234m) in health funding from USAID in 2023 – ranking third after Nigeria which received $368m and Tanzania with $337m.

a3815.speaker: Atul Gawande, USAID’s former global health assistant administrator
a3815.speech: posted on X that the agency’s workforce would be slashed from 14,000 to 294 – with only 12 staff assigned to Africa.

a3815.speaker: Eddah Simfukwe Banda, 32-year-old subsistence farmer in Malawi
a3815.speech: says she and her sister-in-law have little option but to pray: “We have to pray as Malawians. Those of us that believe depend on a God who opens doors when one is closed” ; said systemic failures were to blame: “As Malawians, we depend too much on receiving aid. At times we are lazy and squander and rely on other countries to help us. Let this be a lesson that we have to be independent.”

a3815.speaker: World Bank
a3815.speech: According to the World Bank, Malawi is vulnerable to external shocks – including prolonged droughts, cyclones and erratic rainfall.

a3815.speaker: Jean Kaseya, head of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC)
a3815.speech: told BBC Newsday last month that USAID gave $8bn of aid assistance to Africa over the past year: “Seventy-three per cent went to healthcare.”

a3815.speaker: Dr Githinji Gitahi, CEO of Amref Health Africa
a3815.speech: warns that without urgent action, global health security is at risk: “This would require African governments and Africa CDC to increase their own funding, which is almost impossible under the current debt distress conditions” ; “With accelerating outbreaks from climate change and human-environmental conflict, this would leave the world fragile and unsafe - not only for Africa but for everyone.”

a3815.speaker: Winnie Byanyima, head of UNAids
a3815.speech: told the BBC’s Africa Daily podcast this week: “If you take away this major contribution by the United States government, we expect that in the next five years, there’ll be an additional 6.3 million Aids-related deaths” ; “There will be 8.7 million new infections, 3.4 million additional Aids orphans. I don’t want to sound like a prophet of doom, but I have a duty to give the facts as we see them.”

a3815.speaker: Tom Ellman, Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) Southern Africa
a3815.speech: has said in a statement, warning of the dangers of interrupting HIV treatments: “HIV medicines must be taken daily or people run the risk of developing resistance or deadly health complications.”

a4034.speaker: Nonye Ayeni, Executive Director/CEO of the Nigerian Export Promotion Council (NEPC)
a4034.speech: Disclosed that the NEPC has introduced programmes targeted at expanding market access for Nigerian exporters: "The African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) presents Africa with the single most significant economic transformation initiative of our time. With access to a market of over 1.4 billion people and a combined GDP exceeding $3.4 trillion, AfCFTA promises not only expanded trade opportunities but also greater industrial integration, value addition, and job creation." ; "For Nigeria, SMEs are the heart of this opportunity. They account for the majority of our productive base, providing employment, driving innovation, and serving as the backbone of our non-oil economy. To harness AfCFTA's benefits, we must ensure that our SMEs are not just participants, but winners in this new continental marketplace." ; "Also, the NEPC is connecting businesses with funding platforms and reducing barriers that limit their participation in cross-border trade."

a4059.speaker: Dr. Tegbar Yigzaw, physician, public health specialist and Human Resource for Health expert, former Technical Director for the USAID-funded Strengthening Human Resources for Health Project at Jhpiego
a4059.speech: "COVID 19 is a new strain disaster; we never saw such kind of disasters in our lifetime. If we ask how and why the pandemic has a capacity to damage thousands of life's at a time, it does not give time to find the cure, the virus spreads all over the world within a short period of time. It can be said that the pandemic is resulting in the worst damages not only on the health also economically and socially after the Second World War. Within three months the virus has attacked more than a million people in 200 countries, even the developed and wealthy countries which has a strong health system are suffering a lot by the pandemic. For example if we see Italy, it is the second European country to have strong health system, but could not stand the damage of the pandemic, they are asking support from other countries. Most of the countries are taking measures to control the virus through social distancing; countries are locking down their borders, minimize the effect since there is no cure."

a4059.speaker: Dr. Tegbar Yigzaw, physician and public health specialist
a4059.speech: "It is already known that the virus also gets in Ethiopia, we have found out some numbers, but it doesn't mean the victim is only those numbers. We have such a weak health system, we don't have the capacity both in human resources and logistics to serve thousands of patients if the pandemic spreads highly, the other thing is that we don't have the medical supplies and protective materials to health care workers. If the virus continues to spread it will be difficult for us. The most important thing is that we already know how the virus is transmitted from one to another, it makes it easy to do prevention to minimize the damages; the government is working with its full capacity." ; "Both the government and health workers are primarily acting to control the spread, especially by overseeing countries experiences who has successfully control the spread including South Korea and China... but if we see the USA and other European countries they are suffering a lot, they did not respond fast for the spread and prevention." ; "We have to make ready our health centers, health care materials medicines, protective materials... the country cannot serve more than 500 critical patients both in private and government level... we have to be ready by preparing ventilators which are critical in treating the victims, we have to train our health workers about the virus... If it is beyond our permanent health centers, we have to prepare additional temporary centers." ; "One of the measures to prevent the spread is that we have to find out the cases, the real cases and victims of the virus and quarantine them... If someone sees the symptoms they have to isolate themself, they have to go to health centers." ; "We have to keep our distance, avoid hand shacks and touches we have to wash our hands every 20 minutes... Maintain at least 1-meter distance between yourself and anyone who is coughing or sneezing... Stay home if you feel unwell." ; "One of the challenges is, because of the lack of sufficient hospitals and expertise we may focus on the cases of the virus and other patients will be forgotten, so the death may rise not only in the case of the virus but also on other patients."

a4059.speaker: Studies on the virus (cited by Dr. Tegbar Yigzaw)
a4059.speech: suggest that only two peoples are dying per 100 patients, although when the number of the patient rises the number of death also rise.

a4059.speaker: Dr. Tegbar Yigzaw, physician and public health specialist
a4059.speech: "The thing is that the patient may stay normal for some days without showing the symptoms from 5 to 14 days, however, even if the symptoms are hidden the virus can still be transmitted from one to another, checking the high temperature is not the only way to find out whether he/she is a victim or not, so the passengers may seem well when they came, but sow the symptom after joining the public. In my assumption there were two option, one was to minimize our flights especially to those highly affected countries, or to quarantine all the travelers, we are doing this but it was better if we were taking this kind of measures from the beginning."

a4059.speaker: Dr. Tegbar Yigzaw, physician and public health specialist
a4059.speech: "When the pandemic starts highly spreading in the world, associations starts to move to form a task force to help Ministry of Health on the fight against the virus. The task force will help the ministry on the privation and control by assessing different global experiences, how does the virus spread what should be done, who are most masquerade to the virus."

a4060.speaker: Dr Oluwasherimi Ajetumobi, Oyo State Commissioner for Health
a4060.speech: Has said that a total number of 245 suspected cases of the dreaded cholera disease was reported between January 1 to October 7, 2024 with 23 cases confirmed while only one death was recorded during the period ; pointed out that the only death recorded was a patient brought from Lagos, adding that nine (9) patients currently on admission at the Infectious Disease Center, Olodo, Ibadan are responding to treatment and will soon be discharged.

a4060.speaker: Dr Oluwasherimi Ajetumobi, Oyo State Commissioner for Health
a4060.speech: Said a request for approval of the sum of N210,243 million state counterpart fund for the support of the net campaign coming up in May 2025 was also looked into at the meeting ; ”as part of the activities towards the net campaign, there are some things that we need to do and that is the reason for the request. The United States Agency for International Development USAID, initiative has procured a total of 5,670,644 nets for the state and the state is expected to pay a counterpart fund of N210,243.” ; said the counterpart fund is to cater for the micro planning which includes logistics, flag off, net campaign, storage and distribution across the 33 local governments of the state ; ”Just as we know that the burden of severe malaria in Oyo State disproportionately affects the vulnerable population particularly children under five, pregnant women and the elderly.” ; ”Malaria, if happened during pregnancy, can lead to severe outcomes ranging from severe anaemia, miscarriage, and low birth weight.” ; stated that the procurement of the nets cost the USAID the sum of N1,726,214,195, while assuring that every household will benefit from the net distribution exercise with consideration for vulnerable persons.

a4060.speaker: Dr Wasiu Olatunbosun, Oyo State Commissioner for Culture and Tourism
a4060.speech: While addressing newsmen, gave highlights of activities slated for the rest of the year approved by the Executive Council as regards culture and tourism, including the World Twin Festival on October 12, 2024 at Igbooora, the Yemoja festival October 10-27, 2024, the Omilere Alaragbo festival, the Oluyole festival, the Omituntun Cultural Carnival, the Iyake International festival, the Aso-ofi festival and the maiden edition of the Ogbomoso Global Cultural Carnival on December 14-24, 2024, which he described as first of its kind that will bring the sons and daughters of Ogbomoso land from across the globe together.

a4124.speaker: Chuck Schumer, US Senate Majority Leader
